https://mg.co.za/news/south-africa/2026-.text: Evidence leader Matthew Chaskalson detailed WhatsApp exchanges involving taxi boss Jotham “King Mswazi” Msibi and Sergeant Fannie Nkosi in which they discussed an alleged plan to acquire and sell cellphone-interception devices, commonly known as “grabbers”. The devices can be used to eavesdrop on phone calls and extract information from mobile devices. Reviewing WhatsApp messages before the Madlanga Commission of Inquiry, Chaskalson said Msibi, Nkosi, Katiso “KT” Molefe and Steven Motsumi appeared to be involved in a plan to acquire the devices from a Czech Republic company using the South African Police Service as a front. The devices were allegedly intended for sale in eSwatini. Chaskalson referred to a planned demonstration involving phone expert Shaun Jacobs, during which the devices would be showcased. “What will emerge is that Mr Msibi, Sergeant Nkosi and quite possibly Mr Motsumi and Mr Molefe … have a plan to sell grabber technology to the Kingdom of eSwatini,” Chaskalson said. “Of course, that is not what the Czech Republic has been told at all. The Czech Republic has been told that this is a demonstration for the South African Police Service.” The commission was shown correspondence relating to the proposed deal with the Czech company. Some of the documents contained official SAPS stamps. Chaskalson said one of the WhatsApp exchanges from January 2023 involved a supplier saved on Nkosi’s phone as “Sean Jacobs — phone expert”, who had asked whether the “Swazi deal” was still on the table. Nkosi had forwarded the message to Msibi, who replied: “It’s on the table but they have to display. We don’t want to become fools.” Chaskalson said Nkosi had allegedly placed a SAPS stamp on a procurement document to facilitate the deal, which the evidence leader characterised as fraudulent conduct. The commission also examined WhatsApp exchanges between Msibi and Kyle Phillips, a director of tobacco company Carnilinx. The messages allegedly show Phillips seeking Msibi’s assistance after several thefts and hijackings involving cigarette consignments. In one of the exchanges, a person identified as “Ali”, whom Chaskalson described as a suspected robber, communicated with Phillips about the return of stolen cigarette stock. In another exchange, Phillips allegedly offered Msibi “red water”, a substance used in illicit gold processing. Molefe has been implicated in allegations surrounding the murders of musicians DJ Sumbody and DJ Vintos. He is a co-accused with Vusimuzi “Cat” Matlala in a case that is before the Johannesburg High Court. Further evidence shows Motsumi and Msibi planning a trip to Paris and Hamburg for a procurement meeting. They planned to buy an active monitoring system and tactical equipment to the tune of R1.16 million. Msibi was listed as owner of Themy Styles, a security company and Molefe as director. “Again we have a situation where a European dealer in high-tech security surveillance security equipment and the like is being told Mr Motsumi was a representative of the state,” Chaskalson said. “If we can take a step back and take stock of what we are looking at here because it is quite alarming … Mr Msibi, Mr Motsumi, Mr Molefe and possibly Sergeant Nkosi are involved in a commercial project which involves the selling of high-tech surveillance systems and jamming technology.” Chaskalson said Crime Intelligence head Dumisani Khumalo had described Msibi as the former leader of the Big Five cartel, while Molefe was on trial for murder. Molefe’s firearms has been linked to more than 30 murder scenes in Gauteng in the past five years. He said Motsumi was an individual whom the former head of Hawks, Lesetja Senona, had been afraid to mention during his testimony at the commission. “These three men are dealing with foreign companies to get access to grabber technology purporting to represent the state,” Chaskalson said. “They didn't manage in the first case to sell to the eSwatini government [but] they may well have managed in this instance; we don't know,” he said. He said the group had been able to represent the South African state as civilians, allegedly due to their association with Nkosi.

REUTERS/Marco Bello Matthew Rozsa September 22, 2026 | 01:43PM ET When President Donald Trump was elected in 2016, and then reelected in 2024, Americans who opposed him asked a simple and understandable question: What went wrong? Anthony Scaramucci , who briefly served as Trump's communications director during his first term, offers a compelling and highly readable answer to that question in his new book, "All the Wrong Moves." At once brisk and thought-provoking, "All the Wrong Moves" avoids appealing strictly to either Democrats or Republicans and instead digs into the deeper systemic problems that Scaramucci argues led America to the Age of Trump. From America's trade deals with China and forever wars waged without paying for them to bailing out the Wall Street banks that caused the Great Recession, policymakers on both sides created economic conditions that systematically disempowered and alienated the working class. Trump, Scaramucci asserts, was the political consequence of these profound socioeconomic errors. Even if one doesn't fully agree with his arguments, "All the Wrong Moves" is still a Must Read, since it raises and logically supports observations about recent American history that pervasively resonate today. For those who do mostly agree with Scaramucci's points, of course, "All the Wrong Moves" will help them flesh out their positions in future conversations. I interviewed Scaramucci for AlterNet about his book. This interview has been lightly edited for clarity, length and context. Profiting off the White House Rozsa: What is Trump's endgame? In your opinion, how does all of this end in terms of what Trump is trying to do to America right now? Scaramucci: It's a really good question. I think his endgame is to see if he can make another $10 to $20 billion for himself and then pardon himself and his family members. I think that's his endgame. I don't think he has a policy endgame. I don't think he cares a wick about any person that voted for him or even anybody in America. He certainly would like to leave some monuments to himself in Washington. I don't think he'll be successful in knocking down the Kennedy Center . He'll certainly be successful at building that ballroom. It'll remain indeterminate about the Trump arc, the triumph. But Trump wants to name things after himself, he wants to make money, and he wants attention. So look to see those people restored to the White House, Politico, CNN. He'll have to get them restored because they cut his air supply off. Even though he supposedly hates the journalists, he wants them there so he can get eyeballs and attention. But that's it. He doesn't have a policy endgame. He doesn't care about any of that stuff. Rozsa: This makes me think of how you described, in your own words, a Potomac bubble, and how the Potomac bubble insulates people in Washington from the consequences of their actions. How does that bode in terms of people standing up to Trump when they work for him? His White House staff, Republicans in Congress, frankly, the Supreme Court justices who are conservative. Can they break out of that Potomac bubble and stop what Trump is doing to this country? Or based on your experience, is that bubble too thick? Scaramucci: No, they can't do it. This is a failed political class of leaders. This is baby boomers, unfortunately, which I happen to be among. I was born at the tail end. They're a failed group of political leaders, and they only care about their own self-aggrandizement, and they only care about putting their personal power first. If they cared, Kevin McCarthy would've gotten them impeached and he would've gotten McConnell to convict him, and he would've never stood for office in 2024. And again, remember that Trump's rise is concomitant with the failure of the Democratic Party to put up good candidates. They put up a mediocre candidate and they lost to a sitting president, Donald Trump. And Joe Biden. They put up two very disastrous presidential candidates and they lost to him. He's not a popular figure, and very rarely, except for the November '24 election, where he had the consensus of the popular vote, generally he's been below 50 percent. And now look at him today: lowest approval ratings in modern presidential history, or close to right where Richard Nixon was when he resigned. So listen, they won't do it. They're afraid of him. They don't want to get dislodged by somebody at Trump's support. He does have power in the right-leaning primary voting bloc, and those guys are worried about that. What motivates Trump voters Rozsa: And what you said right now is part of why I'm going to recommend your book. I'm letting you know upfront, I read it in less than a day. It is a fast read, and it's insights like that, particularly how the Democratic Party has failed its own voters, that I think people on both sides need to hear, because I 100 percent agree. Scaramucci: Well, first of all, I appreciate you bringing that up, Matthew, because that's exactly what I wanted to write: a book that could be read in a day. There's some humor in it, and it's a nonpartisan observation. Somebody said on Amazon, and I was very grateful for it, that it's an apolitical book. I'm not taking it into the world of tribalism. I'm not taking it into the world of partisan rancor. I'm just saying, "Hey, mistakes were made on both sides. Well-meaning, well-intended people can make mistakes. This is how they go about doing it." And if you can understand what the mistakes are, then we can begin the process of trying to fix them. Rozsa: I would absolutely agree that your book is bipartisan in its approach. There are a couple of points where I want to push back on your book, not in an uncivil way, but simply to spark an interesting conversation. Scaramucci: Please. Let's do it. Rozsa: So at one point, you write, "I know many liberal Democrats who assume that Trump came to power only because his voters are racist, sexist, and homophobic, et cetera. And sure, those qualities exist in this country, obviously, but they're not really what brought us to this point." When I interviewed you for Salon eight years ago , you had a similar observation. I would argue, based on my observation, that a lot of people who support Trump do so primarily because he validates their hatred of trans people, their hatred of gay people, their hatred of women and Black people and immigrants. I do not think that's all of them. I don't even think that's a majority of them, but I would argue it is a sizable minority. What are your thoughts? Scaramucci: Okay. So you might be right. I would have to look at granular data, and you and I would have to hire focus groups and do some polling and then some cross-data. I would say that you're more right today than perhaps in 2018 when we had the interview. I think that the racial divides, the xenophobia, the isolationism have gotten worse. I finished the manuscript of this last summer. I did make some revisions before we went into print. If there were a second edition of this book that I could update instantaneously, I would probably take out what I wrote, because I think you are more right now than what I was feeling maybe a year ago when I was writing that. And I think, to your point, it has gotten worse. Rozsa: Why have your opinions changed on the subject? Scaramucci: Because I'm out in the field and listening, and I try to meet as many pro-Trump supporters as possible. Some of it is racially tinged. Some of it is in what I would call the culture-war bucket: the anti-trans bucket, if you will, the anti-pronoun-usage bucket, the anti-woke bucket, which is intolerant. There's an intolerant strand. I think the first vote was, "Okay, let's try something new. He's an outsider and the current system isn't working for us." And I think the second vote was, "Okay, it wasn't really that bad when he was president, and we don't know who Kamala Harris is," so it was a lesser-of-two-evils vote. But I think what he's done over the last two years has opened up a Pandora's box of intolerance, way, way more so recently than ever before. Trump and Israel Rozsa: I agree with your analysis. I now want to go to a quote from Chapter 8 that I thought was very insightful. You discussed neoconservatives and how their belief that, quote, "the US was now in a historically unique position to exercise immense control over events" and "revived old dreams of US nation-building abroad and injected the dreams with new juice," and was responsible for the second war in Iraq, which was obviously a disaster and which set the precedent for, as you described it, "wars without taxes, wars that we're not paying for." My question is, to what extent do you view Israel and its influence over American politics, and, sadly, its massive human rights violations in Gaza, as contributing to this tendency in American foreign policy? Scaramucci: Okay, it's a very complex question. So I'm going to say that Netanyahu clearly influenced Donald Trump to unilaterally strike Iran. And so we can then say, is it Netanyahu's fault or is it Donald Trump's fault? Let me just say that it's Donald Trump's fault that we struck Iran. I don't think the war's working, and I don't even think it met the Israeli interests or the American interest. The outcome that was promised is not happening, which is that we would decapitate the regime and the regime would fall and then the country would secularize. As it relates to Israel, not to sound overly cynical, but Israel has done better in terms of surviving with failed bordering states. If you have a failed state in Syria, a failed state in Lebanon, it seems to work for Israel. Having a failed Iran, in their minds, is probably better than having a radicalized Iran. I think that's where the interests diverged between the United States and Israel. I don't think the United States wants a failed state in Iran. They would like something that's more akin to being in the family of nations. So Israel has had an influence on us. I think the AIPAC lobby has been a strong lobby. AIPAC has the right, by the way; these are US citizens, and they do have the right to lobby the Congress. And so we could then debate whether or not... if you don't like that lobby and you don't like the influence that they've had with these political leaders, then vote for the people that are opposing them who are not influenced by that lobby. But to me, the broader point on Israel is that we have a long-term strategic alliance, and of course the United States under Harry Truman was very helpful in terms of making sure there was a formation of the state of Israel. And Netanyahu would not like me to say this, and this could perhaps even be controversial, but I think that the Prime Minister of Israel has more than one role. Yes, it's to protect the safety and the sovereignty of the state of Israel, but whether he likes it or not, he's almost like an international brand representative for international Jewry. And so this humanitarian crisis that has been caused in Gaza has hurt the brand. Listen, I grew up in a Jewish neighborhood. I see myself as a philo-Semite. I have supported Jewish causes and charities related to Jewish causes my whole life. But I'm a realist. Has the brand been hurt by what's going on in Gaza? Yes, it has. If people want to pretend that it hasn't, they can, but I would be more interested in figuring out how to fix the brand. And this is the last point that I would make: antisemitism, broadly and historically, when measured and examined over 5,000 years, invariably is a precursor to mass violence. And the people that want to scapegoat Jews, when the Jewish domino falls, it tips into other dominoes. Many people think, "Oh, well, they're going after the Jews. I'm not a Jew, that's okay for me." But it isn't, because you're hitting a minority class and you're knocking a domino eventually into another minority class. You think they're going after other people, but the way this stuff works is they come after you too. And so we need to stop it. So I'm not a big fan of antisemitism. I don't love Bibi Netanyahu's strategy in Gaza. We can debate the definitions of what happened there. I just think it has caused a humanitarian crisis and it's hurt the brand. Rozsa: I agree with what you said. Personally, the term that I would use is genocide. I know many Jews find that upsetting, but my response is, I agree with what you said about Netanyahu being, whether he likes it or not, a brand representative for Jews. And unfortunately, he is a terrible representative, not only because he's perpetrating a genocide, but because he is corrupt, and in my opinion has intentionally lengthened this war because he knows as soon as it's over, he faces corruption charges. In my opinion, just as America needs to elect Democrats in the upcoming midterms to put a check on Trump, Israel needs to replace Netanyahu with Gadi Eisenkot. I'm sure you're familiar with him. He's the head of the Yashar! party. Scaramucci: Yep. I've actually met him. I met him way back in 2018. Rozsa: Do you think he'd be a good prime minister, or at least a better one than Netanyahu? Scaramucci: Better. I think he's more cognizant of what I'm saying and you're saying. I'm more careful with the word, the definition of genocide, because of the triggering effects of it. I'll tell you something, and you know this from your political reporting: let's say I'm fiscally conservative and socially liberal. If I use those words, I've now turned off 50 percent of the people, because the Republicans spent billions of dollars on the word "liberal" to spoil it for the group of people, and the Democrats have spent billions of dollars on the word "conservative." So if I say I'm socially inclusive and fiscally responsible, I'm able to reach people better. Do you see what I'm saying? And so I don't use the word genocide, because the minute you use it, you're polarizing both sides. I would rather say that it's a humanitarian crisis, which I think is factually accurate. And I would like to say that the humanitarian crisis has gotten out of hand, and as a result it's hurt the brand. The minute I use the word genocide, given my profile, it'll raise lots of consternation. And I'll tell you something, and you can see this: my podcast partner, Katty Kay, whom you may often see on Morning Joe , used the word genocide. The Israeli government listens to the show. They wrote to the BBC, which she's an employee of, which is linked to the British government, and made her apologize on the air and issue a retraction, because she's not allowed to make statements like that as a, quote-unquote, quasi-governmental employee of the United Kingdom. She made the statement, she issued the retraction, but let's not take away from what the problem is, which is why I focus on the words "humanitarian crisis." A Democrat who was a better fiscal conservative than Trump Rozsa: I appreciate you being so thorough. I now want to move on to another subject from your book. You discussed President Bill Clinton and his administration and the various ways that he disempowered the working class and helped facilitate the housing crisis. At the same time, when I interviewed one of his top economic advisers, Dr. Robert Shapiro , he pointed out, and this is a quote, "Bill Clinton is the only president in 50 years who actually governed based on mainstream economics." And in an article accompanying that interview, he pointed out that Clinton was able to deliver a balanced budget, create four large surpluses, and nearly 23 million

But Europe has well-founded fears about that Paul Taylor Berlin’s allies are right to be wary of a sudden surge in German military spending that shuns cooperation with them Thu 8 Oct 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 03.17 EDT Share W hen the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, visited the White House earlier this year for a high-stakes meeting with Donald Trump, he invited a Washington-based German researcher little known outside expert circles to a private dinner. Liana Fix had caught his eye with a forthright essay in the journal Foreign Affairs warning of the perils of Germany becoming “Europe’s next hegemon”, whose military dominance may come to scare its neighbours and divide Europe once again. That concern might seem far-fetched after three decades since the fall of the Berlin Wall, during which a peace-loving reunited Germany let its armed forces wither and rust, prided itself on being a “civil power” and preached a gospel of military restraint. Yet the combination of a sudden surge in German rearmament, growing doubts over the United States’ willingness to remain the guarantor of European security through Nato, and the rise of the far-right nationalist Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party, currently leading in opinion polls, has reignited old anxieties among Berlin’s neighbours, especially Poland and France. Fix, a historian and senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, has built her argument into a timely and incisive book, Germany Rearmed: The Return of War and the End of Illusions . Among the fallen myths she skewers are not just the delusion that economic interdependence would make Russia a benign partner for Europe, which collapsed with Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, but also the end of what she calls “the illusion of the west”, which had been central to Germany’s identity and foreign policy since 1945. “It is not that Germany wants to leave the west, but the west seems to be abandoning Germany, in particular the US-led western order,” Fix told me in an interview. To guard against any hegemonic temptation, she urges Berlin to anchor its future military power in closer European unification by helping to finance European defence through joint defence bonds, embracing a Europeanisation of the continent’s national arms industries, and deepening the integration of the Bundeswehr into European armed forces. There is little sign so far that Merz, whose first defence strategy, released in April, vowed to make Germany Europe’s strongest conventional army by 2039 , is heeding her advice. Struggling with unpopularity, economic stagnation and a rising cost of living, the conservative chancellor has ruled out issuing eurobonds to fund European defence. His government scrapped two big arms cooperation projects with France – a next-generation fighter aircraft and a tank. Planned arms purchases worth €123.3bn notified to parliament last month are overwhelmingly from national and US industries, with only scraps for European partners. To be sure, all Berlin’s armed forces are committed to Nato, unlike France’s, and it has invited allies to join its European Sky Shield air and missile defence programme. Germany is the biggest donor of financial and military assistance to Ukraine. It is working with the UK on deep precision strike weapons. And it has stationed a brigade in Lithuania to help protect Europe’s eastern flank in the first permanent deployment outside its territory since 1945. Defence industrial nationalism is by no means confined to Germany. France and the UK are equally protective of their national arms makers. The EU’s defence commissioner, Andrius Kubilius, laments that up to 80% of European defence purchases are made by direct awards with national prime contractors without a competitive tender, exploiting a security exemption in the EU treaty. The fact that German rearmament coincides with a severe slump in core manufacturing industries such as cars, chemicals and machinery is an extra reason to “buy national”. But Berlin, once on the frontline of east-west confrontation, is now cushioned by a buffer zone of central European allies and should have an interest in helping them invest in their own defence. For practical reasons, it’s better to help equip friends and neighbours to intercept drones and missiles before they reach Germany rather than waiting to shoot them all down over Berlin and Frankfurt. Fix is right to argue that because of its dark history and its weight in the middle of Europe, Germany must do more than others to reassure its neighbours and to embed its rearmament in common European industrial, political and military structures. As Timothy Garton Ash has argued in the Guardian, that is what Helmut Kohl achieved a generation ago by anchoring German reunification in a common European currency. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion Otherwise, the question of German power and its political uses is bound to return sooner or later, especially if the Russia-friendly AfD, which opposes assistance for Ukraine and advocates withdrawal from the EU, continues to gain ground in German elections. “The German question is not dead,” Fix told me. “It’s dead in the sense that a militaristic Germany will not re-emerge under a centralised government. But the German question can also just be a question of dominance and of balance. And this is the thinking we unfortunately have to revive.” Paul Taylor is a senior visiting fellow at the European Policy Centre Explore more on these topics Germany Opinion Europe Arms trade Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) European Union comment Share Reuse this content Comments ( … ) Sign in or create your Guardian account to join the discussion Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
